_meta: A smooth 16-sample intensity gradient, split into two 8-sample blocks and compressed the way JPEG compresses an image -- each block transformed by the discrete cosine transform (DCT), its coefficients quantized, and inverse-transformed back -- used to show that the DCT itself is lossless and it is the independent per-block quantization that both loses detail and creates the blocking artifact at the seam between blocks. The DCT rewrites a block as a sum of cosine waves of increasing frequency; for smooth content almost all the energy lands in the lowest-frequency coefficients (the DC average and the first alternating-current term), which is why an image compresses -- you can store a few coefficients instead of all the samples. That transform is exactly invertible: DCT followed by inverse DCT returns the block to the last bit. The loss enters only at quantization, where each coefficient is rounded to a multiple of a step size to save bits: a large step zeroes the small high-frequency coefficients (blurring detail) and coarsely rounds the surviving low-frequency ones. Because each block is quantized on its own, two neighbouring blocks that were part of one smooth gradient round to slightly different reconstructed levels, so a discontinuity appears at the block boundary that was not in the original -- the blocking artifact, the tell-tale 8-pixel grid of over-compressed JPEGs. A finer step keeps the gradient and the seam smooth; a coarser step saves more space but makes both the detail loss and the blocking worse. signal is the pixel row; block_size is the transform block length; fine_step and coarse_step are two quantization step sizes. The DCT coefficients, the lossless round trip, the reconstruction error, and the block-boundary jump under each step are computed. Stdlib only.
